{"entity": "Capacitor", "type": "artifact", "description": "The Capacitor is a passive two-terminal electrical component used to store energy electrostatically in an electric field when voltage is applied across its terminals. Functionally, capacitors serve multiple roles in electronic circuits: they store electrical energy, filter or smooth signals (e.g., in power supply decoupling or audio applications), and contribute critically to the behavior of frequency-dependent networks. When connected in series with an inductor, the capacitor forms part of resonant LC circuits; when placed in parallel with a resistor, it constitutes an RC network—where it influences impedance magnitude, phase shift between voltage and current, and overall frequency response. Its voltage-dependent behavior is fundamental in timing, coupling, and filtering applications, and its passive nature means it neither generates nor amplifies energy but instead absorbs and releases it cyclically. Across all descriptions, the capacitor is uniformly characterized as non-dissipative in ideal operation (though real-world equivalents exhibit parasitic resistance and inductance), and its schematic placement—whether below an inductor, in series with it, or in parallel with a resistor—reflects its versatile integration into diverse circuit topologies.<SEP>Capacitors are passive electronic components with various capacitance values used in circuit experiments.<SEP>A capacitor with capacitance 2 F is used in the experiment to study frequency-dependent impedance behavior.<SEP>A capacitor is a passive electrical component that stores energy in an electric field, presenting infinite impedance in DC steady state and frequency-dependent capacitive reactance in AC.<SEP>A capacitor is a passive electrical component with capacitance C = 2 F, whose AC impedance and voltage–current relationship are measured in the experiment."}

{"entity": "Oscilloscope", "type": "artifact", "description": "The oscilloscope is an electronic test and measurement instrument fundamental to electrical engineering, electronics education, circuit analysis, and laboratory experimentation. It serves both practical and pedagogical functions by enabling real-time capture, display, processing, and analysis of electrical waveforms—including sine, triangle, rectangular, and calibration signals—as well as dynamic signal behavior during circuit testing, troubleshooting, and instructional experiments. As a core component of test benches, it is routinely used alongside signal generators and function generators to observe time-domain and frequency-domain characteristics of signals across diverse technical and educational contexts.

Physically and functionally, the oscilloscope features a display screen—often capable of rendering multiple simultaneous waveform traces—and a structured control interface organized into vertical (voltage/amplitude scaling), horizontal (timebase/sampling rate), trigger (synchronization via internal or external sources, slope-trigger configuration, adjustable trigger position), and run-control sections. Input/output ports include analog channels (commonly labeled CH1–CH4), external trigger inputs, probe compensation terminals, USB connectivity, and logic analyzer interfaces, supporting versatile analog and digital signal acquisition. Its operational interface consistently highlights essential elements including Acquire settings menus, trigger configuration screens, time-base controls, and channel-specific voltage scaling, all critical for precise signal capture and parametric adjustment. Additional capabilities include tracking mode, automatic measurement mode, and cursor-based waveform analysis—facilitating rapid quantification of frequency, amplitude, period, rise time, and other signal integrity parameters.

The oscilloscope is used to observe and record voltage waveforms across various points in circuits—such as Uad, Ucd, Uab, Ubc, and Uac in filter networks—as well as to analyze transient processes in microdifferentiation and integration circuits. It supports specialized analyses including phase relationship assessment via Lissajous figures and is especially valuable for examining repetitive waveforms, though modified techniques can extend its utility to non-repetitive or single-shot events. Schematic representations frequently depict it as a large rectangular block labeled “示波器” (Chinese for “oscilloscope”) or “到示波器” (“to oscilloscope”), with probes marked “X” and “Y” connected to key circuit junctions such as amplifier outputs and low-pass RC filter networks—emphasizing its role as an external, integrated measurement device. While some references contextualize the oscilloscope implicitly—through labels in circuit diagrams, image captions, or lesson plan directives—all converge on its indispensable role: providing accurate, real-time observation, manipulation, and interpretation of waveform phenomena. Its educational utility is further reinforced by schematic line-art depictions incorporating Chinese-labeled functional elements or commercial identifiers such as Rigol, reflecting both universal instrumentation principles and specific hardware implementations.<SEP>An oscilloscope is an electronic test instrument used to observe and analyze the waveform of electrical signals, including transient responses.<SEP>An oscilloscope is used to observe rectangular pulse voltage and resulting waveforms in the experiments."}
